passage: So Devika, remember when Sir announced in assembly that my poem won the district round? Everybody turned and clapped. I was grinning like an idiot, but my hands went into my pockets and I looked at the floor. Then I said, loudly, "It was just luck, ask Devika, she gave me the rhyme." People laughed and Sir looked confused. After that I wanted to disappear. Later, in the corridor, Sir said quietly, "I meant it, Wasim. The last verse was really good." And that made my chest feel warm without anyone watching. I'm not against praise. I just can't take it with two hundred people looking.

qa.q: What did Sir announce in assembly?
qa.a: He announced that Wasim's poem won the district round.

qa.q: Why did Wasim joke and look at the floor when praised?
qa.a: Wasim was pleased but uncomfortable being the centre of two hundred people's attention. The joke about luck may have been a way to deflect the attention, not a rejection of the praise.

qa.q: How could Sir give Wasim recognition next time?
qa.a: He could say a private word or write a short note, since the corridor comment felt warm to Wasim.

qa.q: How might Sir have read Wasim's joke in assembly?
qa.a: He may have thought Wasim did not care or was being modest, which is why he looked confused.

grounding: A teenager who is pleased by praise squirms in public, and a quiet private word suits better.

passage: I'm writing this because our class teacher asked us to observe something kind. During Friday's maths class, Ms Jain said, "Indu got the highest score and her method was very neat." Indu grinned for about a second, then rolled her eyes, pushed her notebook away and said, "Anyone could have done it." Her neck went red. The boys near me whistled and she laughed too loudly. I can't say what she felt, she might not like being noticed, or might have been shy. After class, Ms Jain quietly put a sticky note on her desk. Indu read it, folded it and tucked it into her pencil case, and she was smiling on the way out. Vaibhav.

qa.q: Who got the highest score in Friday's maths class?
qa.a: Indu got the highest score.

qa.q: What might Indu's red neck and eye-roll suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: They suggest she felt pleased but self-conscious about being noticed in front of others. It could also be shyness, and Vaibhav cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did Ms Jain do that seemed to work?
qa.a: She left a private sticky note on Indu's desk, which Indu kept and smiled about.

qa.q: How might the classmates who whistled see Indu's reaction?
qa.a: They may think she is enjoying the attention or does not care, though she may be squirming inside.

grounding: A teen looks pleased yet squirms at public praise, and a quiet private note suits better, seen by an observer.

passage:
Monday: Santosh Sir read Zainab's essay aloud in English class and called it "the best I've read in five years." Zainab smiled for half a second, then slid down in her chair and said, "He's paying me, guys." Everyone laughed. Her ears were bright red.
Wednesday: Sir mentioned the essay again at assembly practice, in front of three sections. Zainab studied her shoelaces and pulled her hood up. Later, her friend heard her mutter, "Please let him forget it."
Friday: Santosh Sir handed back her notebook quietly. Inside was a note: "Your essay made me think about my own grandmother. Keep writing. No need to reply."
Zainab read it on the bus. She smiled properly this time, alone at the window, and read it twice. That weekend she wrote a second essay, and she left it on his desk herself.

qa.q: What did Santosh Sir call Zainab's essay on Monday?
qa.a: He called it "the best I've read in five years."

qa.q: What does Zainab's joke and red ears on Monday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was pleased but embarrassed at being praised in front of everyone, so she joked to deflect the attention.

qa.q: Which of Santosh Sir's approaches worked best, and why?
qa.a: The private note on Friday worked best, because it gave her the praise without the social exposure, and she wrote another essay.

qa.q: How might Santosh Sir have read Zainab's reactions on Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: He might have thought she didn't care for the praise, unless he noticed that her discomfort was about the audience, not the compliment.

grounding: The three beats show a teenager squirming at public praise and responding warmly to a quiet private word.

passage:
Lavanya, you're making that face because your coach praised you in front of the team? Let your grandfather tell you something. My name was on everyone's lips once too.
When I was fourteen I found a wallet near the bus depot and took it to the headmaster. At the Monday assembly, in front of six hundred children, he said, "Anirban Ghosh has shown us what honesty looks like." And he made me stand on the stage.
I wanted the ground to swallow me. I grinned like a fool, shrugged, and walked back so fast I tripped on the steps. For weeks the boys called me "Honest Babu."
The thing I remember with pleasure came later. My maths teacher stopped me in the corridor and said quietly, "I heard. Well done." That was all.
That small, private word, Lavanya, I carried for fifty years.

qa.q: What did the headmaster call Anirban at the assembly?
qa.a: He said, "Anirban Ghosh has shown us what honesty looks like."

qa.q: How did Anirban feel standing on the stage?
qa.a: He felt deeply embarrassed and exposed, wanting the ground to swallow him, even though the praise was for something good.

qa.q: Which moment in the story made the praise land well, and why?
qa.a: The maths teacher's quiet "Well done" in the corridor, because it recognised him without an audience or teasing.

qa.q: How might the headmaster have seen that assembly?
qa.a: The headmaster probably thought he was honouring Anirban and teaching the school, without realising how exposed it made a fourteen-year-old feel.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teen squirming at public praise and valuing a quiet private word more.

passage:
Sports day was running two hours late because of rain, and three hundred students were squeezed under one dripping tent. Coach Kishore grabbed the microphone.
"Before the relay, one special mention. Sonali Pawar broke the school record in the 800 metres, and she trained every morning at six, even in the monsoon!"
Everyone turned. Somebody whistled. Sonali gave a quick thumbs up, then buried her face in her towel and said loudly, "It was the rain, the rain pushed me." Laughter. She edged behind a pillar.
Her friend saw her fiddling with her medal ribbon, rolling and unrolling it.
After the relay, with the tent emptying in the drizzle, Coach Kishore stopped by her. "Too much, the mic?"
Sonali nodded, half smiling. "I liked it. Just not with everyone looking."
"Next time I'll tell you first. And I'm proud of you."

qa.q: How late was sports day running?
qa.a: Sports day was running two hours late because of rain.

qa.q: What did Sonali's joking and hiding behind a pillar suggest?
qa.a: It suggested she was pleased but embarrassed by the attention of three hundred people, not that she disliked the praise.

qa.q: What did Coach Kishore do afterwards that helped?
qa.a: He asked her privately if the microphone had been too much and repeated his praise quietly, which suited her better.

qa.q: How might Sonali's friend have read the medal ribbon fiddling?
qa.a: The friend may have seen it as a sign of nerves or discomfort under her joking, though it could also just have been restless energy.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager deflecting public praise with a joke, and a quiet private word landing better.

passage: At Monday assembly in the Lucknow school hall, Jomon Sir held up a sheet and announced, "The best essay in the whole of class ten came from Usha Verma. Come up, Usha." Two hundred heads turned. Usha's cheeks went pink and the corners of her mouth kept twitching upward, but she walked to the stage like it was a punishment, hands balled into her sleeves. "Sir must have mixed up the pages," she said into the mic. Everyone laughed. She laughed too, then stared at her shoes until she could leave. Later, in the corridor, Farah said, "You looked like you wanted to vanish. Did you hate it?" Usha shook her head. "I loved it. I just hated everyone looking." That afternoon Jomon Sir stopped by her desk and said quietly, "Your ending made me think for a long time." Usha didn't joke that time. She said, "Thank you, Sir," and smiled properly.

qa.q: Where did Jomon Sir praise the essay?
qa.a: He praised it at Monday assembly in the Lucknow school hall.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as she walked to the stage?
qa.a: Usha felt pleased but embarrassed by the attention, with a twitching smile and balled hands; the joke deflected the exposure rather than showing dislike of the praise.

qa.q: Which kind of praise suited Usha better, and why?
qa.a: The quiet word at her desk suited her better because it was specific and private, so she could simply enjoy it without everyone looking.

qa.q: How did Farah read Usha's behaviour on stage?
qa.a: Farah thought Usha looked like she wanted to vanish and wondered if she hated it, which shows how squirming at praise can be misread.

grounding: It shows a teenager looking pleased yet squirming and joking when praised in front of peers, and a quiet private word suiting her better.
